questions.q: What does an imperative script require the author to specify that a declarative configuration does not?
options: The cloud provider's name
The exact ordered sequence of steps needed to reach the end result
Any resource names at all
A version number
questions.explain: Imperative scripts are a list of steps run in order, written and sequenced by the author. Declarative configurations describe the end state and let the tool determine the order.

questions.q: In the lesson's Terraform example, how does Terraform know to create the resource group before the storage account?
options: It always creates resource groups first by default
The storage account block references the resource group's attributes, which establishes the dependency
The two resources are listed in that order in the file
You must write a separate 'depends_on' step script
questions.explain: The storage account block reads azurerm_resource_group.dev.name and .location, so Terraform infers that the resource group must exist first.

questions.q: What happens when the Azure CLI script from this lesson is run a second time?
options: Nothing — it recognizes the resources already exist and exits cleanly
It either errors out or attempts to create a duplicate, since it has no memory of what it already did
It automatically updates the existing resources
It deletes the existing resources and recreates them
questions.explain: An imperative script has no built-in memory of prior runs, so rerunning it typically causes an error or duplicate creation attempt.

questions.q: What does it mean for an operation to be 'idempotent'?
options: It can only be run exactly once
Running it repeatedly produces the same result with no unintended side effects
It requires manual approval every time
It only works with declarative tools, never imperative ones
questions.explain: Idempotent means repeated runs of the same operation produce the same outcome — running terraform apply twice in a row with no config changes reports 'No changes.'

questions.q: Why does this course favor a declarative approach for Northbridge Retail's infrastructure?
options: Declarative tools are always faster to execute
Infrastructure needs to exist consistently across environments and be safely re-run without manual step-tracking
Imperative scripts cannot create cloud resources at all
Declarative tools don't require any configuration files
questions.explain: For infrastructure that must stay consistent across dev, staging, and production and be re-run safely, a declarative, idempotent tool like Terraform is a better fit than an imperative script.
